title: [Inside the Newsroom] Why road safety is a budget issue
summary: An ambitious goal to achieve zero road deaths requires adequate funding, and right now Congress has just given it zero allocation

blocks.text: An ambitious goal to achieve zero road deaths requires adequate funding, and right now Congress has just given it zero allocation

I’m Patrick Cruz, a multimedia reporter for Rappler covering transportation, among other beats. Every day, millions of Filipinos navigate a chaotic, congested, and often perilous transport system. But the true cost of our daily commute isn’t just measured in lost hours and lost productivity; some lives are also lost on the road.
In Metro Manila alone, the Metropolitan Manila Development Authority records an average of 239 road crash incidents every single day. That is roughly 10 accidents every hour.

The national picture is even more alarming. According to recent data from the Philippine Statistics Authority, 3,133 people already died due to road crashes from January to April 2026 — not even half a year!
This staggering figure makes road accidents the 13th leading cause of death in the country.

The government acknowledges that this is a crisis. The Philippine Road Safety Action Plan (PRSAP) 2023–2028, led by the Department of Transportation (DOTr), laid down an ambitious target to reduce road traffic deaths and injuries by at least 35% by 2028. It has a long-term vision of zero road deaths.
But here is the glaring disconnect: ambitious goals require adequate funding, and right now the money simply isn’t there.
The DOTr proposed a modest P111.29 million to fund the PRSAP. However, under the House General Appropriations Bill (HGAB), that allocation was reduced to exactly zero.

Similarly, infrastructure designed to protect our most vulnerable road users has been gutted. The Active Transport Bike Share and Safe Pathways Program — essential for protecting cyclists and pedestrians — received a measly P33.9 million allocation. That is a mere 3% of the proposed P1.13 billion needed to build and maintain safe active transport networks.
Without this funding, millions of Filipinos who rely on active transport are left to fend for themselves on fast-moving, heavily motorized thoroughfares.
Advocates are rightfully sounding the alarm. The Move As One Coalition has pointed out that no funding has been provided for road safety for the past three years.

“There’s no funding for road safety for the past three years, which is why we ask the Senate: Please, if you’re really serious in helping prevent road crashes, in making sure that our most vulnerable are protected, fund road safety,” Move As One Coalition representative Lou Gepuela said during the budget deliberations in the Senate.

The road safety budget now sits in the hands of the Senate. Will our lawmakers finally put their money where their mouth is to protect commuters? Or will we see another year of zero funding for a crisis that claims thousands of Filipino lives?
Let’s keep a close eye on how government officials craft our national budget. Follow our #BudgetWatch page for more stories on where your taxes go (and where they don’t). – Rappler.com
